stories.title: The Mango Tree That Hummed
segment_text: The Mango Tree That Hummed. Behind a yellow house, in a quiet lane, there stood an old mango tree. Every evening, when the sky turned the colour of ripe papaya, the tree began to hum. Hmm, hmm, it went, as softly as a grandmother singing.

sat under the tree with a cup of warm haldi milk. "Why do you hum, Mango Tree?" "I hum to help the birds fall asleep," said the tree. "The mynas are chatty, the parrots are giggly, and the little sparrows always want one more story."

listened very carefully. The mynas stopped chatting. The parrots tucked their green heads under their wings. A small sparrow yawned a tiny yawn. The breeze joined in, rustling the leaves like a soft dupatta. Far away, a temple bell rang once, and then it rested too.

whispered, "Will you hum for me as well?" "Of course," said the tree. "Breathe in, slow as a leaf floating down. Breathe out, slow as the moon rising." Hmm, hmm, went the mango tree, and the whole lane drifted gently off to sleep.

Behind a yellow house, in a quiet lane, there stood an old mango tree. Every evening, when the sky turned the colour of ripe papaya, the tree began to hum. Hmm, hmm, it went, as softly as a grandmother singing.

{FAV} sat under the tree with a cup of warm haldi milk. "Why do you hum, Mango Tree?"

"I hum to help the birds fall asleep," said the tree. "The mynas are chatty, the parrots are giggly, and the little sparrows always want one more story."

{FAV} listened very carefully. The mynas stopped chatting. The parrots tucked their green heads under their wings. A small sparrow yawned a tiny yawn.

The breeze joined in, rustling the leaves like a soft dupatta. Far away, a temple bell rang once, and then it rested too.

{FAV} whispered, "Will you hum for me as well?"

"Of course," said the tree. "Breathe in, slow as a leaf floating down. Breathe out, slow as the moon rising."

Hmm, hmm, went the mango tree, and the whole lane drifted gently off to sleep.

stories.title: The Sleepy Monsoon Cloud
segment_text: The Sleepy Monsoon Cloud. High above the rooftops floated a small grey cloud named Baadal. All day long Baadal had watered the fields, filled the ponds and tapped a happy rhythm on the tin roofs. Pitter, patter, pitter. Now the evening had come, and Baadal felt heavy and tired.
looked up from the window. "Hello, little cloud. You look sleepy." "I am," sighed Baadal. "But I do not know where clouds should rest."

thought for a moment. "Maybe the hills would hold you, like a pillow." So Baadal drifted towards the green hills. The hills were round and soft, and they smelled of wet earth and tea leaves. The frogs sang a slow song from the ponds. A peacock folded its long tail and settled on a branch. Baadal let out one last gentle shower, just enough to make the leaves shine. Then the cloud spread out across the hilltops like a warm grey shawl.
waved goodnight. The rain had stopped, the air was cool, and the whole valley breathed slowly in and out. Down below, every window glowed, and one by one, the lights went out.

Now the evening had come, and Baadal felt heavy and tired.

{FAV} looked up from the window. "Hello, little cloud. You look sleepy."

"I am," sighed Baadal. "But I do not know where clouds should rest."

{FAV} thought for a moment. "Maybe the hills would hold you, like a pillow."

So Baadal drifted towards the green hills. The hills were round and soft, and they smelled of wet earth and tea leaves. The frogs sang a slow song from the ponds. A peacock folded its long tail and settled on a branch.

Baadal let out one last gentle shower, just enough to make the leaves shine. Then the cloud spread out across the hilltops like a warm grey shawl.

{FAV} waved goodnight. The rain had stopped, the air was cool, and the whole valley breathed slowly in and out. Down below, every window glowed, and one by one, the lights went out.

stories.title: The Little Diya
segment_text: The Little Diya. On the windowsill sat a little clay diya with a tiny golden flame. It was the smallest lamp in the house, and sometimes it wondered if it was bright enough.

knelt beside it after dinner. "Your light is lovely," came a kind whisper. "But the big lamps are so much brighter," said the diya. "The big lamps are for reading and cooking," said Amma from the kitchen. "A little light is perfect for bedtime."

watched the flame sway, left and right, left and right, as calm as a boat on a pond. It made soft shadows on the wall: a cat, a kite, a curled-up moon. Outside, the neighbours' diyas glowed too, a whole street of small, warm lights. Each one kept a little circle of the night cosy. The diya stood up a bit taller. "Then I will keep watch," it said, "so the dark feels friendly."
snuggled under the blanket, eyes growing heavy. The tiny flame flickered, steady and gold, all through the quiet night, keeping everyone company until morning.

stories.title: The Tea Garden Elephant
segment_text: The Tea Garden Elephant. In the hills of Assam, among rows and rows of tea bushes, lived a gentle elephant called Moti. Moti had big flappy ears and walked so softly that not a single leaf was ever crushed. One evening the mist rolled in, white and silky.
was walking home along the path when Moti appeared, swinging a slow, friendly trunk. "Would you like a ride to the edge of the garden?"

climbed up carefully and held on. Sway, sway, went Moti, step by careful step. The tea bushes smelled fresh and green. Fireflies blinked like tiny lanterns in the mist. They passed the old banyan tree, where a family of monkeys was already asleep in a heap. They passed the stream, which was singing to itself in a low, bubbly voice. At the gate, Moti knelt down so the ride could end gently. "Thank you, Moti." "Thank you for the company," rumbled the elephant. "Now it is time for both of us to sleep."
waved, and Moti turned back into the soft white mist, ears flapping slowly, like the wings of a very big, very sleepy bird.

In the hills of Assam, among rows and rows of tea bushes, lived a gentle elephant called Moti. Moti had big flappy ears and walked so softly that not a single leaf was ever crushed.

One evening the mist rolled in, white and silky.

{FAV} was walking home along the path when Moti appeared, swinging a slow, friendly trunk. "Would you like a ride to the edge of the garden?"

{FAV} climbed up carefully and held on. Sway, sway, went Moti, step by careful step. The tea bushes smelled fresh and green. Fireflies blinked like tiny lanterns in the mist.

They passed the old banyan tree, where a family of monkeys was already asleep in a heap. They passed the stream, which was singing to itself in a low, bubbly voice.

At the gate, Moti knelt down so the ride could end gently. "Thank you, Moti."

"Thank you for the company," rumbled the elephant. "Now it is time for both of us to sleep."

{FAV} waved, and Moti turned back into the soft white mist, ears flapping slowly, like the wings of a very big, very sleepy bird.

stories.title: The Houseboat and the Moon
segment_text: The Houseboat and the Moon. On the calm backwaters of Kerala, a wooden houseboat rocked gently on the water. Coconut palms leaned over the edges as if they were listening. The moon came up, round and silver, and laid a shining path across the water.

lay on a soft mat on the deck, watching the stars come out. "Look," said Appooppan, pointing. "The moon has come to say goodnight." The water lapped against the boat. Lap, lap, lap. A kingfisher made one last flight across the river and settled in its nest. Somewhere on the shore, a cow gave a slow, sleepy moo.

counted the lights on the far bank: one little lamp, two little lamps, three. Each one was a home where someone was getting ready for bed. The boatman began a quiet song in Malayalam, a lullaby as old as the river. The melody floated over the water and joined the hum of the crickets.
felt the boat rock, slowly, slowly, like a cradle. The moon kept watch from above, the river kept moving below, and in the middle, warm and safe, sleep arrived.

{FAV} counted the lights on the far bank: one little lamp, two little lamps, three. Each one was a home where someone was getting ready for bed.

stories.title: The Night Train to Nani's Village
segment_text: The Night Train to Nani's Village. The night train left the big city station with a long, friendly whistle. Inside, the carriage was warm and the berths were made up with crisp white sheets.

climbed onto the middle berth and pressed a nose to the window. The city lights slid away, and soon there were only fields and the wide, dark sky. The train began its rhythm. Chuk-chuk, chuk-chuk, chuk-chuk. It sounded like a heartbeat, steady and calm. A chai-wallah passed by, calling softly so as not to wake anyone. Further down, a baby was already asleep in a cloth hammock, swinging gently with the train.

thought about Nani's village: the courtyard with the tulsi plant, the big brass pot, the buffalo named Rani, and Nani's soft hands making rotis in the morning. "We will be there when you wake up," said Papa, tucking in the sheet. The train crossed a long bridge over a quiet river. The moon followed along, keeping pace like a friend.
yawned. Chuk-chuk, chuk-chuk, went the train, carrying everyone through the night, all the way to morning.
